moments.title: Three ways to write a function
moments.text: $f(x)=x^2-2$, $f: x\mapsto x^2-2$ and $y=x^2-2$ all describe the same rule. Use whichever your textbook uses.

moments.title: Evaluate by substitution
moments.text: $f(3)=7$, $g(-2)=1$ and $h(24)=5$. Find the function, then substitute the input for $x$.

moments.title: Domain and range
moments.text: The domain is the set of possible inputs ($x$ values). The range is the set of possible outputs ($y$ values).

moments.title: Domain and range of a quadratic
moments.text: $f(x)=x^2-2$ goes left and right forever, so $x\in\mathbb{R}$. It bottoms out at $-2$, so $y\ge-2$.

moments.title: A straight line
moments.text: $g(x)=x+3$ goes on forever in every direction, so both domain and range are all real numbers.

moments.title: A square root function
moments.text: $h(x)=\sqrt{x+1}$ starts at $x=-1$ and only gives non-negative outputs: domain $x\ge-1$, range $y\ge0$.

moments.title: A composite is a function of a function
moments.text: In $f\circ g$, the output of $g$ becomes the input of $f$.

moments.title: Find $f\circ g$
moments.text: Write $f$, and where it has $x$, put in $g(x)=x+3$. The result is $(x+3)^2-2$.

moments.title: Find $g\circ f$
moments.text: Start with $g$ and put $f(x)$ where $x$ was: $x^2-2+3=x^2+1$. A different order gives a different function.

moments.title: Inverse functions and their notation
moments.text: The inverse of $f$ is written $f^{-1}$. Start from $y=f(x)$.

moments.title: Swap $x$ and $y$, then solve for $y$
moments.text: The first step is always to swap $x$ and $y$. Then use algebra to make $y$ the subject.

moments.title: The inverse of $h$
moments.text: From $y=\sqrt{x+1}$: swap, square both sides, subtract 1. $h^{-1}(x)=x^2-1$.

moments.title: The inverse is a reflection
moments.text: The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the graph of $f$ reflected in the line $y=x$.

notes.title: Restricting the quadratic domain
notes.text: The video finds a square-root inverse for $f(x)=x^2-2$ without first restricting the original domain. On all real numbers the function is not one-to-one.
notes.write: Restrict to $x\ge0$ to obtain $f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x+2}$ with domain $x\ge-2$; choosing $x\le0$ gives the negative branch.

notes.title: Domain of an inverse
notes.text: The video finds an inverse for $h(x)=\sqrt{x+1}$ but does not explicitly state its domain.
notes.write: The original range is $[0,\infty)$, so $h^{-1}(x)=x^2-1$ has domain $x\ge0$.

ican.text: I can form and evaluate composite functions in the correct order.
I can determine the domain of a composite by checking both functions.
I can decide when a function has an inverse and restrict its domain when necessary.
I can find an inverse and state its domain and range.
I can check inverse relationships and interpret the reflection in the line $y=x$.

ku.text: $(f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))$: apply $g$ first and then apply $f$ to the result. In general $f\circ g$ and $g\circ f$ are different.
For $f(g(x))$ to exist, $x$ must be in the domain of $g$ and $g(x)$ must be in the domain of $f$. Derive the domain before cancelling or simplifying expressions.
A function has an inverse function on a given domain when it is one-to-one there. Graphically, every horizontal line meets its graph at most once.
To find an inverse, write $y=f(x)$, interchange $x$ and $y$, and solve for $y$. Select a branch consistent with the original domain.
The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$; the range of $f^{-1}$ is the domain of $f$. Their graphs are reflections in $y=x$.
The inverse undoes the function on the appropriate domains: $f^{-1}(f(x))=x$ for $x$ in the domain of $f$, and $f(f^{-1}(x))=x$ for $x$ in the range of $f$.
$f^{-1}(x)$ denotes the inverse function, not the reciprocal $1/f(x)$. Also, $\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$ for real $x$.

misc.better: Evaluate the inner function first: $x\to g(x)\to f(g(x))$.

misc.weak: Simplifying a composite gives $x$, so every real input is allowed.
misc.better: Check the original inner and outer domains; algebraic cancellation does not restore excluded inputs.

misc.weak: Every quadratic has an inverse function on all real numbers.
misc.better: A quadratic is not one-to-one on all real numbers. Restrict its domain to one side of its vertex before finding an inverse function.
The principal square root is nonnegative, so $\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$.

misc.weak: The inverse has the same domain as the original.
misc.better: The inverse domain is the original range and the inverse range is the original domain.

terms.text: The result of applying one function to the output of another, subject to both domain conditions.
A function is one-to-one if different inputs cannot give the same output.
A function that reverses a one-to-one function, with domain equal to the original range.
The nonnegative square root; for example, $\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$.

worked.prompt: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}$ with domain $x\geq1$, and $g(x)=x^2+1$ with domain $x\in\mathbb R$.

parts.label: a
parts.a: $f(g(x))=\sqrt{(x^2+1)-1}=\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$. Since $g(x)=x^2+1\geq1$ for every real $x$, the domain is $\mathbb R$.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find $(g\circ f)(x)$ and its domain. Compare it with part (a).
parts.a: $g(f(x))=(\sqrt{x-1})^2+1=x$ for $x\geq1$. The original input must lie in the domain of $f$. Although $|x|$ and $x$ agree for $x\geq1$, the two composites have different domains and are therefore different functions.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Find $f^{-1}$, stating its domain and range.
parts.a: Put $y=\sqrt{x-1}$, so $x=y^2+1$ with $y\geq0$. After interchanging variables, $f^{-1}(x)=x^2+1$ for $x\geq0$. Its range is $[1,\infty)$.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Explain why $g$ has no inverse function on $\mathbb R$, then give an inverse if its domain is restricted to $x\geq0$.
parts.a: $g(2)=g(-2)=5$, so $g$ is not one-to-one on $\mathbb R$. On $x\geq0$ it is one-to-one and its inverse is $g^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x-1}$ for $x\geq1$.

kq.q: How do you find a composite’s domain?
kq.model: Require the input to be valid for the inner function and require its output to be valid for the outer function. Keep both restrictions after simplification.

kq.q: Why does a quadratic need a restricted domain to have an inverse function?
kq.model: On its full real domain, points equally far from the vertex have the same output. Restricting to one side makes the function one-to-one.

kq.q: How are a function and its inverse connected graphically?
kq.model: Swap input and output coordinates: $(a,b)$ on the function corresponds to $(b,a)$ on the inverse, reflecting the graph in $y=x$.
